text: Briana Collette Scurry, born on September 7, 1971, is an American retired soccer goalkeeper. She was the starting goalkeeper for the United States women's national soccer team at the 1995 World Cup (3rd place), 1996 Summer Olympics (gold medal), 1999 World Cup (champions), 2003 World Cup (3rd place), and the 2004 Summer Olympic Games (gold medal). She played in the semi-final and playoff for third place in the 2007 Women's World Cup (3rd place). Scurry was a founding member of the WUSA, playing three seasons as starting goalkeeper for the Atlanta Beat from 2001 to 2003. Her career total of 173 international appearances is the second most among female soccer goalkeepers and the fifteenth most of any American female player, as well as the thirty-second most among all women. Scurry was elected to the National Soccer Hall of Fame on August 3, 2017, becoming the first woman goalkeeper and the first black woman to receive the honor. She is openly gay and married Chryssa Zizos, CEO of Live Wire Strategic Communications, LLC, on June 1, 2018. In 2022, she released her best-selling memoir, *My Greatest Save*, and was the subject of the CBS feature-length documentary *The Only*, released that year. Scurry was born in Minneapolis, Minnesota, to parents Ernest and Robbie Scurry and is the youngest of nine children, with three brothers and five sisters. She played goalie for the Anoka High School Tornadoes for four years and was instrumental in their Minnesota State Championship win in 1989, which ended in a shootout victory. In high school, she ran track and played floor hockey and softball, but basketball was her first and deepest love. She was named Anoka High School's Athena Award winner, High School All American, and Minnesota's top female athlete. In 2010, she was inducted into the Minnesota State High School Hall of Fame, and in September 2011, she was named to the inaugural class of the Anoka High School Hall of Fame. Scurry attended the University of Massachusetts Amherst, completing her four-year collegiate career with 37 shutouts in 65 starts and a career record of 48–13–4 with a 0.56 goals-against-average. She split time in the net in 1992, starting 13 games and earning seven shutouts, and played three games as a forward that year. In 1993, she helped lead the UMass Minutewomen to a 17–3–3 record, to the semifinals of the NCAA Women's Soccer Championship, and titles in the Atlantic 10 Conference regular season and tournament. In her senior season, she started all 23 games, recorded 15 shutouts, and had a 0.48 goals-against-average, the third best in the nation. She was named National Goalkeeper of the Year in 1993 by the Missouri Athletic Club Sports Foundation and was a 1993 second-team All-American, All-Northeast Region, and All-New England first-team selection. Scurry was a founding player for the Atlanta Beat in the Women's United Soccer Association (WUSA), the world's first women's professional league, where she served as starting goalkeeper for the three seasons (2001–2003). She helped the Beat reach two WUSA Championship Games and was named Goalkeeper of the Year in 2003. On March 13, 2009, she was named to the preseason roster of the Washington Freedom in the inaugural season of Women's Professional Soccer (WPS), but suffered a season-ending concussion early in the 2010 season and announced her retirement on September 8, 2010. Scurry was a goalkeeper for the United States women's national soccer team from 1994 to 2008, earning 173 caps, starting 159 games, and finishing her international career with a record of 133–12–14 and 71 shutouts. Her first appearance for the US team was on March 16, 1994, against Portugal, during which she recorded her first shutout. In her first year, she earned seven shutouts in 12 starts. She was a member of the gold-medal-winning US Women's National Team at the 1996 Olympic Games in Atlanta, starting and playing every minute of the team's five matches, conceding only three goals. In the 1999 Women's World Cup, she played every minute, allowing only three goals and recording four shutouts, and saved one penalty during the shootout in the final against China, leading to the United States' victory. Following the World Cup, she announced her intention to play in the WNBA. She started for the US in the 2003 FIFA Women's World Cup and the 2004 Summer Olympic Games, played two matches in the 2007 FIFA Women's World Cup, and was the alternate goalkeeper on the 2008 Olympic Team. On June 23, 2008, coach Pia Sundhage announced that Scurry would not be on the Olympic team; her last match for the United States was on November 5, 2008, against the Korea Republic. While playing in the Women's Professional Soccer league in 2010, she suffered a traumatic brain injury when a player from the opposing team collided with her knee into her right temple, leaving her temporarily totally disabled and dealing with severe depression. To address her symptoms, she underwent occipital nerve surgery in 2013. Scurry has since rebuilt her life and become an advocate for increased concussion awareness and research, testifying before Congress twice. In 2011, she was appointed general manager of the WPS franchise magicJack. In February 2021, The Washington Post reported that Chelsea Clinton, Jenna Bush Hager, Dominique Dawes, and Scurry were part of an investment group investing in the Washington Spirit. Scurry served as part of the rotation of studio commentators for ESPN's telecasts of the 2011 FIFA Women's World Cup. Since 2021, she has served as a broadcast analyst for CBS soccer coverage, including serving as the lead desk analyst for the 2022 CONCACAF W Championship. On December 6, 2017, she was announced as the First Assistant Coach of the Washington Spirit and would serve as Technical Advisor for the Spirit Academy programs in Maryland and Virginia. Scurry appeared as a fictionalized version of herself in the 2000 film *Air Bud: World Pup* and was the subject of the 2022 Paramount Plus documentary *The Only*, directed by Anthony J. Cortese, which featured interviews with other USWNT players such as Mia Hamm, Brandi Chastain, Kristine Lilly, and Abby Wambach.
